1.title: A throne for a subway rider
1.text: At 116 St–Columbia University, Michelle Greene’s Railrider’s Throne is an oversized steel chair designed to make waiting commuters feel special.

2.title: Same name, different station
2.text: Gun Hill Rd on the 2 sits on White Plains Road. The 5’s Dyre Avenue branch has another Gun Hill Rd station, near Sexton Place and Dewitt Place—check the line as well as the name.

3.title: Harlem’s history on the platform
3.text: Willie Birch’s Harlem Timeline at 135 St brings neighborhood residents together with figures including Langston Hughes and Charlie Parker. Billie Holiday appears on the uptown side in indigo.

4.title: An imaginary room at Yankee Stadium
4.text: Helene Brandt’s Room of Tranquility at 161 St–Yankee Stadium creates the illusion of a quiet room revealed behind sliding tile walls, beside Vito Acconci’s architectural artwork.

5.title: An express becomes a neighborhood shuttle
5.text: During typical late-night service, the 5 shrinks to a Bronx shuttle between Eastchester–Dyre Av and E 180 St. Its familiar daytime trip through Manhattan and Brooklyn does not run overnight.

6.title: A forest made by blacksmiths
6.text: Elder Av’s Bronx Trees uses 20 hand-wrought steel grilles to represent native trees of the Bronx River area. Different species appear on the northbound and southbound platforms.

6X.title: Express in the Bronx, local in Manhattan
6X.text: The diamond 6’s limited weekday peak-direction express stops include Parkchester, Hunts Point Av, and 3 Av–138 St. Its express identity is the Pelham segment, rather than Lexington Avenue in Manhattan.

7.title: The subway’s westward expansion
7.text: The 7 was extended to 34 St–Hudson Yards in 2015, carrying its Flushing route farther west than Times Square. The extension added subway access to the developing Hudson Yards neighborhood.

7X.title: A ballpark platform puzzle
7X.text: Mets–Willets Point, a stop for both local and diamond 7 service, has an unusual combination of two side platforms and one island platform. Its listed entrances include Citi Field’s Jackie Robinson Rotunda.

A.title: One letter, three Queens destinations
A.text: The A has branches to Ozone Park–Lefferts Blvd and Far Rockaway–Mott Av, plus limited peak-direction rush-hour trips to Rockaway Park. The destination on the train matters as much as the letter.

B.title: Yoko Ono brings the sky underground
B.text: At 72 St on Central Park West, Yoko Ono’s SKY turns photographs of clouds into intricate mosaics. Messages including Dream and Imagine Peace interrupt the rush of the commute.

C.title: Extinct animals have their own color code
C.text: At 81 St–Museum of Natural History, For Want of a Nail depicts extinct animals in grey and living animals in color. The station artwork was developed with the museum above it.

D.title: Art powered by arriving trains
D.text: At 34 St–Herald Sq, David Provan’s Yab-Yum consists of red wind paddles designed to spin and flutter in the air pushed by approaching and departing trains.

E.title: There really is a subway alligator
E.text: Tom Otterness’s Life Underground at 14 St includes a bronze alligator emerging from a sewer to swallow a man. The tiny sculptures hide beneath stairs, beside pillars, and on railings.

F.title: A subway station high above the city
F.text: Smith–9 Sts, served by the F and G, is the highest elevated station in the New York City Transit system. It opened in 1933 on the Culver Line viaduct.

FX.title: A diamond on a usually local line
FX.text: The F’s Brooklyn express variant uses a diamond bullet. MTA’s station guide identifies 7 Av as a local-and-express station, where the route shares platforms with the G.

G.title: A crosstown route that skips Manhattan
G.text: The G links Queens and Brooklyn without making a stop in Manhattan. Its official station list runs from Court Sq to Church Av, offering a different path through the city’s subway network.

M.title: Queens at both ends
M.text: The M’s weekday route starts and ends in Queens, but travels through Manhattan and Brooklyn between Forest Hills–71 Av and Middle Village–Metropolitan Av. Staying in one borough does not mean staying within it for the ride.

J.title: The skyline gives way to the tunnel
J.text: On the J, Marcy Av is an elevated station with side platforms; the next Manhattan stop, Delancey St–Essex St, is underground with a side platform and an island platform. One trip changes both setting and platform layout.

Z.title: A partner that skips a different set of stops
Z.text: During J/Z skip-stop service, stations such as 121 St and Norwood Av receive Z service while their J service is listed outside rush hours. The pair divides some stops rather than simply using the same express stopping pattern.

L.title: Signals that let trains run closer together
L.text: The L is one of the subway routes using communications-based train control. This modern signaling technology follows trains more precisely, allowing closer spacing than the legacy signal system.

N.title: Below the street, beneath the open sky
N.text: Many N stations in southern Brooklyn—including 8 Av and 18 Av—sit in an open cut. They are below street level in a trench, yet exposed to daylight rather than enclosed in a tunnel.

Q.title: A New Year’s Day subway debut
Q.text: On January 1, 2017, the first phase of the Second Avenue Subway opened. Q service began using the new 72 St, 86 St, and 96 St stations on Manhattan’s East Side.

R.title: A tunnel rebuilt after 27 million gallons of flooding
R.text: Superstorm Sandy filled part of the R’s Montague Tube with about 27 million gallons of saltwater and debris. After its long-term repair closure, the tunnel reopened in September 2014.

W.title: The weekday member of the Broadway family
W.text: The W’s regular service is weekdays only. MTA lists it alongside the N at Astoria stations, but it disappears from the typical late-night map rather than running around the clock.

GS.title: A small shuttle with a much bigger connection
GS.text: The 42 St Shuttle reconstruction eliminated platform-to-train gaps and improved accessibility. It also added a free connection between the Times Square routes and the Sixth Avenue lines at Bryant Park.

FS.title: One platform for either direction
FS.text: Park Place on the Franklin Avenue Shuttle has just one side platform, unlike the two-platform layout at neighboring Botanic Garden. This compact Brooklyn stop is also listed as wheelchair accessible.

H.title: A shuttle with ground-level bookends
H.text: The Rockaway Park Shuttle’s Broad Channel and Beach 116 St terminals are at ground level. Between them, its Beach 90 St, Beach 98 St, and Beach 105 St stations are elevated.

SI.title: A half-century wait for new trains
SI.text: In 2024, Staten Island Railway introduced R211S cars—the railway’s first new train cars in more than 50 years. The change replaced a generation of equipment familiar to island commuters.
